metaData.originalTitle: Beyond extract_text: The Two Layers of a PDF That Drive RAG Quality
metaData.title: Beyond extract_text: The Two Layers of a PDF That Drive RAG Quality
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article argues that high-quality RAG parsing requires two layers: first, understanding a PDF's nature (source software, metadata, TOC) and second, extracting page-level content (text, images, tables, columns) with a short LLM-written summary to bridge the gap between structure and meaning.
metaData.summary: This article is the first part of the parsing brick in a series on building enterprise RAG systems. It argues that effective PDF parsing for RAG requires two distinct layers. The first layer, covered here, focuses on understanding the document's nature: classifying its source software (e.g., Word, LaTeX, scanner), reading its declared metadata and native table of contents, and using these signals to route the document to the correct extraction strategy. The second layer analyzes page-level content, distinguishing native text from OCR layers, detecting images, vector tables, and multi-column layouts. A key innovation is the 'parsing_summary': a single, cached LLM call that produces a short factual summary of the document type, main subject, and key fields. This summary, placed in the question parser's system prompt, solves common RAG failures like the 'what is the name?' problem on a CV. The article uses PyMuPDF (fitz) for all extraction and provides concrete Python code for source detection, column analysis, and page classification. It emphasizes that structural signals (render mode, image coverage) are more reliable than statistical thresholds for making parsing decisions.

mainPoints.point: PDF parsing for RAG has two distinct layers: document nature and page-level content.
mainPoints.explanation: The first layer identifies the document's origin (source software, metadata) to route it to the correct strategy. The second layer extracts and classifies content on each page (text, images, tables, columns).

mainPoints.point: A short, cached LLM summary at parse time bridges the gap between structure and meaning.
mainPoints.explanation: A single LLM call produces a 'parsing_summary' with doc_type, typical_fields, and a factual summary. This is cached and injected into the question parser's system prompt, enabling it to answer questions like 'what is the name?' on a CV.

mainPoints.point: Structural signals (render mode, image coverage) are more reliable than statistical thresholds.
mainPoints.explanation: The article uses render mode 3 to detect OCR layers and 95% image coverage to detect scanned pages, arguing these structural flags are more robust than character-count heuristics.

mainPoints.point: Column detection should annotate line position rather than attempt perfect reading order recovery.
mainPoints.explanation: The pragmatic approach is to label each line as 'left', 'right', 'single', or 'multi' based on its x-coordinate cluster. This allows downstream stages to filter by column position, which is especially useful for structured documents like invoices.

keyQuotes: A PDF is two documents stacked on top of each other: the declared signals (metadata, native TOC, source software) and the page-level content (text vs scan, images, tables, columns, page profile).
The difference between a parser that ships a flat string and a parser that ships something downstream code can query is right here, in the signals it bothered to record.
Each signal saved at parse time becomes a column the rest of the pipeline reads.

relatedArticles.title: Hybrid Search and Re-Ranking in Production RAG
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents a production-grade approach to improving RAG retrieval quality by combining hybrid search (BM25 + dense vectors) with cross-encoder re-ranking and metadata filtering, supported by real-world evaluation metrics.

relatedArticles.title: Beyond the Vector Store: Building the Full Data Layer for AI Applications
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article argues that production AI applications require a hybrid data layer combining vector databases for semantic retrieval with relational databases for transactional integrity, metadata management, and security.

relatedArticles.title: Stop Treating AI Memory Like a Search Problem
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article critiques the conventional 'store-and-retrieve' approach to AI memory, proposing a lifecycle-based system with decay, contradiction detection, confidence scoring, compression, and expiry to manage memory like a human brain rather than a static archive.

relatedArticles.title: Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Anthropic launches Claude Fable 5, a generally available Mythos-class model with state-of-the-art capabilities, alongside Claude Mythos 5 for trusted cybersecurity partners, with new safeguards to mitigate misuse risks.

relatedArticles.title: Introducing workspace agents in ChatGPT
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI introduces workspace agents, a new class of shared, long-running AI agents within ChatGPT for business teams, designed to automate complex workflows, integrate with organizational tools, and operate under enterprise-grade controls.

relatedArticles.title: Building an Evaluation Harness for Production AI Agents: A 12-Metric Framework From 100+ Deployments
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents a comprehensive 12-metric evaluation framework for production AI agents, distilled from over 100 enterprise deployments, covering retrieval, generation, agent behavior, and production health.

relatedArticles.title: OpenAI Introduces GPT-5.5: A New Class of Intelligence for Agents
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI announces GPT-5.5, a new model designed for complex goal understanding and autonomous task completion, now available in ChatGPT and Codex.

relatedArticles.title: Your ReAct Agent Is Wasting 90% of Its Retries — Here’s How to Stop It
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article identifies a critical architectural flaw in ReAct-style LLM agents where hallucinated tool names waste the majority of retry budgets, and proposes three structural fixes—error taxonomy, per-tool circuit breakers, and deterministic tool routing—to eliminate this waste and improve production reliability.

relatedArticles.title: Andrej Karpathy on Code Agents， AutoResearch， and the Loopy Era of AI
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Andrej Karpathy explores the paradigm shift from manual programming to agent orchestration, the automation of AI research, and the profound implications for software engineering and education.

relatedArticles.title: Embeddings Aren’t Magic: The Predictable Failure Modes of RAG Retrieval
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically debunks the magic of embeddings in RAG systems, demonstrating through reproducible experiments that embeddings excel at public vocabulary tasks but predictably fail on enterprise-specific terms, negation, magnitudes, and answer relevance, advocating for upstream filtering over stronger models.
